title: Astronomy on Tap Leiden Monday: Euclid Telescope Dark Matter Talks Pair Galaxy Shapes With Voids
excerpt: Euclid telescope dark matter research takes center stage Monday, Nov. 23, at Astronomy on Tap Leiden, a free English-language evening in the Netherlands. Two speakers cover galaxy shapes, cosmic voids and weak lensing, while Euclid’s first data release is public but its weak-lensing products are
content:
Two researchers who work with data from the European Space Agency's Euclid telescope will give free talks in English on dark matter and galaxy environments at Galerie Café Leidse Lente in Leiden, the Netherlands, on Monday, Nov. 23, starting at 2:00 p.m. ET (8:00 p.m. local time).

The evening, hosted by Astronomy on Tap Leiden, falls less than two weeks after ESA released Euclid's first major data batch on Nov. 12. Anyone who cannot make it to Leiden can watch the recording that the organizers say they will upload to YouTube afterward, though they give no date for it.

The speaker names, talk titles and abstracts come from one source, the event calendar of the Netherlands Research School for Astronomy (NOVA). Leiden University's calendar and the organizers' website confirm the date, time, venue and event title but name no speakers.

Leiden Event Is Free, Runs in English and Starts at 2:00 p.m. ET Monday

Astronomy on Tap Leiden is a group of professional astronomers connected to Leiden Observatory. Its events are free, given in English and open to all ages and backgrounds, with games and quizzes alongside the talks. Neither the NOVA listing nor Leiden University's event page mentions registration or tickets.

The listing describes two astronomy talks plus quiz-style games with science prizes. It does not publish a running order, talk lengths or a break. The organizers say the talks start at 20:00 sharp and ask attendees to arrive early to get in, save a seat and buy a drink at the bar.

NOVA lists the venue as Galerie Café Leidse Lente, while Leiden University's calendar and the organizers' site call the same Haagweg 4 address Cultuur Cafe Leidse Lente. The NOVA listing puts paid parking at Haagweg 8.

The NOVA listing labels the start time CEST, but the Netherlands returned to standard time (CET, UTC+1) on Oct. 25, so 20:00 local time equals 19:00 UTC and 2:00 p.m. ET.

Neumann Fits Shapes to Galaxies and Asks Where Their Light Blobs Point

Dennis Neumann, a PhD student at Leiden Observatory, will give "Light and dark: The cosmic tug of war." His listed bio says he fits shapes to galaxies to work out which direction they face, a question the bio frames as where galaxies' "light blobs" point.

His abstract starts from the figure that about 95% of the universe is dark matter and dark energy, which no telescope sees directly. That share is the sum of roughly 27% dark matter and 68% dark energy in the standard cosmological model. The abstract also says Euclid is building a map of the cosmos reaching about 11 billion years into the past. A University College London release and a 2023 Leiden University interview instead describe Euclid as tracing about 10 billion years of cosmic history, a difference the talk may clarify.

Leiden University's staff directory lists Henk Hoekstra, professor of observational cosmology, as Neumann's supervisor. Hoekstra leads Euclid's weak-lensing group and is one of its four cosmology coordinators.

Same Galaxy Shapes Carry Dark Matter Signal and Environment Signal

Shape measurement is how Euclid turns starlight into a dark-matter map. Dark matter's gravity bends passing light, but the distortion is too small to see in any single galaxy and shows up only as a statistical alignment across many background galaxies. The catch is that galaxies are not round to begin with: their intrinsic ellipticity runs roughly 3 to 300 times larger than the lensing distortion, so analysts must average over enormous samples.

Euclid's visible-light camera, VIS, has about 600 million pixels and measures how galaxies are deformed. Its near-infrared instrument, NISP, supplies distances through a slitless spectrometer. The telescope has a 1.2-meter (3.9 ft) primary mirror and orbits near the Sun-Earth second Lagrange point, about 1.5 million km (932,000 miles) beyond Earth's orbit.

Galaxy orientation is a signal in one field and a nuisance in another. Lensing analysts treat intrinsic alignment, a tendency of galaxies to line up because of the large-scale structure around them, as one of the dominant contaminants of weak-lensing measurements. Euclid's Quick Data Release, which covered 63.1 square degrees, found massive early-type galaxies aligned with projected cosmic filaments along their long axes. Read together, those two facts link Neumann's shape work to the environment science in Awad's talk, though no source says the two talks address each other. Whether the Q1 alignment matters for lensing measurements is a question the study's abstract leaves open.

Awad Studies Galaxies From Crowded Clusters to Nearly Empty Voids

Petra Awad, according to the listing's speaker bio, is a postdoctoral developer for the Euclid telescope who writes code to analyze its images and studies how galaxies form and evolve. Her talk, "It takes a Universe to raise a galaxy: How cosmic neighbourhoods shape galactic lives," covers how a galaxy's surroundings relate to its shape, size, color and star formation.

Leiden University's staff directory lists a Petra Awad at Leiden Observatory under the job title education and research technician. The listing calls the speaker a postdoctoral developer, and neither source explains the difference.

The two ends of that range are physically distinct. Galaxy clusters hold roughly 100 to 1,000 galaxies bound by gravity. Voids are regions whose average density falls below one-tenth of the universe's average, by one working definition, though astronomers have no single agreed definition.

A Euclid Collaboration paper submitted May 28 lists a "P. Awad" as the 26th of 296 authors. The listing does not say this is the same researcher, so the connection is unconfirmed.

Euclid Simulation Forecasts Void Galaxies Merge Later, Not Less Often

The paper, "Euclid preparation: Probing galaxy evolution within cosmic voids in Euclid-like simulations," tests what Euclid should find using a simulated sky built to mimic the Euclid Deep Survey as planned for its first data release. It selects galaxies glowing in hydrogen-alpha light between redshifts 0.4 and 1.8, the range Euclid's slitless spectroscopy can observe. ESA says Euclid scientists will hunt for hydrogen-alpha in the spectra to measure galaxy distances. The authors find voids with REVOLVER, an enhanced version of the ZOBOV algorithm that builds Voronoi cells from the galaxy distribution.

In the simulation, galaxies near void centers are less massive, more actively forming stars and more disk-dominated than galaxies in dense regions. Void galaxies do not merge less often: the study's abstract reports a comparable merger frequency but says mergers happen later than in dense regions. In the full text, galaxies in the lowest-density regions reach 50% and 90% of their observed stellar mass 0.5 to 1 billion years later than galaxies in denser regions. The mass differences are statistically significant but small, about 0.1 dex in median stellar mass.

The result is a forecast, not an observation. The simulated selection favors star-forming galaxies, so quenched systems, especially in dense regions, are underrepresented, and the sample is roughly 60% to 80% complete. The authors argue that Euclid's first release will have the statistical power to detect these trends, but that conclusion rests on a simulation that covers only about 40% of the Euclid Deep Field footprint. Real-data context is thinner so far: Euclid's Quick Data Release found that, at fixed stellar mass, the share of early-type galaxies rises with local density for galaxies below roughly 63 billion solar masses, though the authors caution that the morphology classification relies on galaxy colors.

What Does Euclid's First Data Release Contain, and What Is Still Missing?

DR1-Foundation, released Nov. 12, captures light from more than a billion objects over about 13 months of observations. It includes more than 900 million galaxies, about 15,000 strong gravitational-lens candidates, more than 60 million quasar candidates and spectra from more than 160 million sources. The release covers about 1,900 square degrees, or 14% of the sky area Euclid will survey over its six-year mission, and totals roughly 1.7 petabytes in total. The release's overview paper lists 1,975 square degrees from the Wide Survey plus 77 from the Deep Fields, which sum to 2,052, a difference that may explain why reported areas vary.

The lens figure counts candidates, not confirmed lenses. The catalog lists 15,072 high-confidence candidates: 6,073 graded "sure lens" and 8,999 graded "probable lens." Researchers searched about 68 million of the release's roughly 900 million sources using five machine-learning models, about 7,000 citizen scientists and 67 strong-lensing experts. A further 9,010 "possible lens" systems carry lower confidence still.

The weak-lensing products come later. Full DR1, due in mid-2027, will add weak-lensing observations and calculations of how galaxies and clusters fit into the cosmic web, according to ESA. The DR1 overview paper says June 2027, while ESA says exact dates will come later. Independent coverage notes the November release does not announce a new measurement that settles what dark matter or dark energy are. That timeline means the shape and environment science both speakers describe is still moving from simulations and early releases toward full-survey data.

Astronomy on Tap Leiden Meets Monthly, and November Looks Like Its Last 2026 Edition

The Leiden series meets on the last or second-to-last Monday of most months. The 2026 schedule lists eight editions: Jan. 19, Feb. 16, March 30, April 13, June 22, Sept. 28, Oct. 26 and Nov. 23, with the May 25 edition canceled. October's edition was titled "The Universe's Ghosts and Ripples". The organizers' site shows no December date, so Monday looks like the last edition of the year.

Leiden's chapter held its first edition on March 27, 2017, at Grand Café de Burcht.

A reader in Leiden can hear how galaxy shapes and galaxy neighborhoods connect to Euclid's dark-universe goals at no cost, and a reader elsewhere can watch the recording once the organizers post it. Either way, the evening is best understood as a preview: Euclid's first dataset is public, its weak-lensing and cosmic-web products are due in mid-2027, and the void and alignment results discussed here are, so far, mostly forecasts and early-release findings.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Astronomy on Tap Leiden suitable for people with no astronomy background?

The organizers say all ages and backgrounds are welcome, and the format is informal talks, games and quizzes by professional astronomers in a local café.

Can I watch Astronomy on Tap Leiden if I cannot travel to the Netherlands?

The organizers say they will upload a recording afterward to the Astronomy on Tap Leiden YouTube channel. They have not said when Monday's recording will go up.

Why do galaxy shapes matter for both dark matter and galaxy evolution?

A galaxy's shape is the raw measurement in weak lensing, where small distortions across many galaxies map dark matter. It also records the galaxy's surroundings: Euclid's early data found massive early-type galaxies aligned with cosmic filaments, and lensing analysts must control that intrinsic alignment.

What is a cosmic void?

A cosmic void is a vast, largely spherical region between filaments of galaxies with very low average density, typically 30 to 300 million light-years across. Galaxies inside voids tend to be less massive, more actively forming stars in the Euclid-like simulation described above, though real-data tests are still ahead.
